prompt: Explain how the U.S. Supreme Court works using only bass-fishing tournament metaphors. Keep going well past the point where it makes sense.
response:
The U.S. Supreme Court is like the biggest bass-fishing tournament on the calendar: only a tiny number of anglers get invited onto this lake, the stakes are enormous, and whatever gets weighed at the end can change how everybody fishes for years.

The “lake” is the Constitution and federal law. It is huge, old, full of hidden structure, strange drop-offs, and spots that look shallow until your lure disappears into a constitutional trench. Everybody argues about where the good water really is.

The nine Justices are the tournament judges, elite anglers, and final weigh-in officials all at once. They do not usually go out looking for random fish. Instead, cases are brought to them like bass in livewells from lower-court tournaments. Most of those fish never make it onto the Supreme Court stage. The Court has a very selective “weigh-in card,” and if four Justices think a case is a trophy-sized legal bass, they grant certiorari — basically saying, “All right, back the boat in, we’re fishing this point.”

Lower courts are like regional bass circuits. They fish the same general lake system, but sometimes one circuit says the bass are biting on crankbaits, another says only jigs count, and a third says that what you are calling a bass is actually a submerged log with rights. When the circuits disagree, that is called a “circuit split,” which is like three tournament directors using three different measuring boards. The Supreme Court may step in to standardize the ruler before everyone starts weighing in catfish wearing largemouth jerseys.

The lawyers are the anglers making their casts. Their briefs are tackle boxes: full of precedents, statutes, constitutional arguments, footnotes, spinnerbaits, emergency worms, and one odd-looking lure they swear worked in 1897. Each side tries to convince the Justices that its bait matches the hatch of the law. A strong argument is a perfectly skipped jig under a dock. A weak argument is casting a topwater frog into a parking lot and calling it originalism.

Oral argument is the moment when the anglers stand on the front deck while nine extremely experienced tournament officials fire questions like wind gusts across the reservoir.
